cards.heading: Transport layer jobs
cards.body: TCP and UDP carry data between applications. Port numbers identify the application: a well-known destination port for the server (such as 443) and a random ephemeral source port (49152 and up) for the client. IP address plus port is a socket. A connection is identified by four values: source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port. Two browser tabs to the same server are kept apart by their different ephemeral source ports.

cards.heading: TCP: reliable and connection-oriented
cards.body: TCP sets up a session with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), numbers every byte, acknowledges what arrived, retransmits what didn't and reorders segments. Windowing gives flow control: the receiver says how much it can take before the sender must wait for an ACK. A session closes with FIN/ACK. If a segment isn't acknowledged in time, the sender retransmits it. A graceful close uses the FIN flag (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK, a four-way close); RST aborts a connection at once.

cards.heading: UDP: fast and connectionless
cards.body: UDP just sends datagrams: no handshake, no acknowledgements, no retransmission, no ordering, and an 8-byte header (TCP's is 20+). It suits real-time traffic such as voice and video, where late data is useless, and short query/response exchanges such as DNS. Voice uses UDP because retransmitted audio would arrive too late to be useful. TFTP and SNMP use UDP; FTP and SMTP need TCP.

cards.heading: Well-known ports
cards.example:
TCP 20/21 FTP     TCP 22 SSH      TCP 23 Telnet
TCP 25 SMTP       TCP 80 HTTP     TCP 443 HTTPS
UDP 53 DNS (TCP for zone transfers)
UDP 67/68 DHCP    UDP 69 TFTP     UDP 123 NTP
UDP 161/162 SNMP  UDP 514 Syslog
